# Today

1. **PCA** as a tool (what it is / isn’t)  
2. **Effect sizes and Resampling** (magnitude matters)  
3. **PGLS** (what it is / isn’t)  
4. **Multivariate PGLS / phylogenetic MANOVA**  

---

# The core idea

.pull-left[
Biological datasets often violate "standard stats" assumptions because:

- Variables are correlated (multivariate structure)
- Species share ancestry (non-independence)
- Sample sizes are modest, uncertainty matters

So we use a toolbox:

1. **explore/visualize** differences
2. **quantify** differences
3. **model** differences
]

.pull-right[
<img src="https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-019-41290-2/MediaObjects/41598_2019_41290_Fig3_HTML.png" width="500">
]
---

# Part 1

## PCA as a Tool

---

# Intuition: PCA without Math

.pull-left[
Imagine a cloud of points in 2D:

- If the cloud is stretched diagonally, there is a **dominant direction**.

- PCA finds that direction (**PC1**) and then a perpendicular direction (**PC2**).

**PC1** = direction with the most variation  

**PC2** = next most, but forced to be orthogonal to PC1
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://towardsdatascience.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/1QinDfRawRskupf4mU5bYSA.png" width="500">

]

---

# Intuition: PCA without Math

.pull-left[
Imagine a cloud of points in 2D:

- PC1 describes axes of most variance

- PC2 second most

- PC3 third most

- etc.
]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://towardsdatascience.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/1QinDfRawRskupf4mU5bYSA.png" width="500">

]

---
# PCA answers questions like…

.pull-left[
- "What are the **main ways** organisms vary?"
- "Do multiple traits change together as a **package** (i.e., integration) ?"
- "Can we visualize complex data in 2–3 dimensions?"
]


.pull-right[
<img src="https://towardsdatascience.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/1QinDfRawRskupf4mU5bYSA.png" width="500">


<img src="https://towardsdatascience.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/1LKTwaVmP4Dqxb-N3iD3CHw.png" width="500">


]



---

# PCA is Limited

.pull-left[
PCA is **not**:

- A hypothesis test
- A phylogenetic method (by default)
- A causal explanation (“PC1 is selection”)

PCA is a **summary** of covariance patterns.

]

.pull-right[
<img src="https://towardsdatascience.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/1QinDfRawRskupf4mU5bYSA.png" width="500">


<img src="https://towardsdatascience.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/1LKTwaVmP4Dqxb-N3iD3CHw.png" width="500">

]

---

# Loadings: what makes PC1 and PC2?

.pull-left[
```{r,eval=F}

data(iris)
pca_iris <- prcomp(iris[,1:4])
loadings <- as.data.frame(pca_iris$rotation) %>%
  rownames_to_column("trait")

loadings
```

Interpretation idea:

- A loading tells you which original variables contribute to each PC.
- Big absolute values = big contributors.
]

.pull-right[

```{r,echo=F}

data(iris)
pca_iris <- prcomp(iris[,1:4])
loadings <- as.data.frame(pca_iris$rotation) %>%
  rownames_to_column("trait")

loadings
```

]

---

# Caution: scale matters

.pull-left[
- If traits have different units or ranges, PCA can be dominated by “big” variables.
- `scale. = TRUE` often makes sense for mixed units.

]

.pull-right[
Try it:

```{r}
pca_unscaled <- prcomp(iris[,1:4], scale. = FALSE)
summary(pca_unscaled)
```
]

---
# PCA & Biological Meaning

Our job is to connect statistics to biology:

- Does PC1 look like “size”?
- Does PC2 look like “shape” independent of size?
- Are there groups (ecology, clades) separated?

**PCA suggests patterns; it doesn’t prove mechanisms.**

---

# Part 2  

## Effect sizes and Permutation

---

# Why effect sizes?

.pull-left[
In regressions:

- A small effect can be "significant" with huge N.  
- A large effect can be “non-significant” with small N.

Effect sizes help you answer:

> "Is this difference biologically meaningful?"

]

.pull-right[
```{r, echo=F}
set.seed(1)
x <- seq(0,100,length.out=100)
y1 <- 100+x*rnorm(length(x),mean=10)
y2 <- 100+x*rnorm(length(x),mean = 11)

tibble(x=x,y1=y1,y2=y2) %>% 
  pivot_longer(y1:y2) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x,value,col=name))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```
]

---

# Why effect sizes?

.pull-left[
In regressions:

- A small effect can be "significant" with huge N.  
- A large effect can be “non-significant” with small N.

Effect sizes help you answer:

> "Is this difference biologically meaningful?"

]

.pull-right[
```{r, echo=F}

set.seed(1)
x <- seq(0,100,length.out=5)
y1 <- 100+x*rnorm(length(x),mean=10)
y2 <- 100+x*rnorm(length(x),mean = 13)

tibble(x=x,y1=y1,y2=y2) %>% 
  pivot_longer(y1:y2) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x,value,col=name))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```
]


---

# Common ES metrics

- Mean difference (raw units, or scaled **Z values**)
- Standardized mean difference (**Cohen’s d**)*
- Variance explained (**R²**, partial R²)
- Regression slope (units of Y per unit of X)

*`geomorph`'s functions
---

# Permutation Test: “shuffle labels”

Permutation is great for testing **whether the observed pattern could arise by chance**.

Example question:

- “Are groups A and B different?”

Permutation logic:

- If group labels are arbitrary under H0, shuffling them should not change results much.

---

# Permutation p-value for mean difference

```{r}
A <- rnorm(100,mean = 3,sd=1)
B <- rnorm(100,mean = 3.1,sd=1)
obs <- mean(B) - mean(A)
AB <- c(A, B)
lab <- c(rep("A", length(A)), rep("B", length(B)))

perm <- replicate(5000, {
  lab_p <- sample(lab)
  mean(AB[lab_p == "B"]) - mean(AB[lab_p == "A"])
})

p_perm <- mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))
c(obs = obs, p_perm = p_perm)
```
---

# Permutation p-value for mean difference

```{r}
A <- rnorm(100,mean = 3,sd=0.2)
B <- rnorm(100,mean = 3.1,sd=0.2)
obs <- mean(B) - mean(A)
AB <- c(A, B)
lab <- c(rep("A", length(A)), rep("B", length(B)))

perm <- replicate(5000, {
  lab_p <- sample(lab)
  mean(AB[lab_p == "B"]) - mean(AB[lab_p == "A"])
})

p_perm <- mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))
c(obs = obs, p_perm = p_perm)
```
---

# Resampling takeaway

**Permutation: how surprising is this under random assignment?**

Often more intuitive than "black box" formulas.

Important in `geomorph` functions (`iter=999`, how many random reassignments)

---

# Part 3 
## PGLS: what it is (and is not)

---

# Why phylogeny matters

.pull-left[
Species are not independent data points:

- Related species tend to be similar
- That similarity is *expected* under many evolutionary models

If we ignore this, we can:

- Underestimate uncertainty
- Get "false significant" results
]

.pull-right[
<img src="https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-019-41290-2/MediaObjects/41598_2019_41290_Fig3_HTML.png" width="500">
]
---

# PGLS in plain language

.pull-left[
PGLS is regression where:

- Residuals are allowed to be correlated
- The correlation structure comes from the phylogeny (closely related = more correlated)
- Correlation structure determined by branch lengths (time) and a model of trait evolution

It’s still regression: estimate slope + uncertainty.
]

.pull-right[
<img src="https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41598-019-41290-2/MediaObjects/41598_2019_41290_Fig3_HTML.png" width="500">
]
---

## What PGLS is NOT

PGLS does **not**:

- "remove phylogeny"
- prove adaptation
- guarantee causal direction (X → Y)

It is a statistical adjustment for shared ancestry.

---

# Simulated example: correlated errors

We’ll simulate a tree and traits evolving under Brownian motion.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
tree <- rtree(60)

# Trait X under BM
X <- fastBM(tree)

# Trait Y depends on X plus phylogenetically structured noise
noise <- fastBM(tree, sig2 = 1)
Y <- 0.8 * X + noise

dat <- tibble(sp = names(X), X = as.numeric(X), Y = as.numeric(Y))
```

---
# Fit OLS vs PGLS

.pull-left[
```{r,eval=F}
# OLS ignores phylogeny
ols <- lm(Y ~ X, data = dat)

# PGLS with Brownian correlation
pgls_bm <- gls(Y ~ X,
               correlation = corBrownian(phy = tree, form = ~sp),
               data = dat,
               method = "ML")

summary(ols)$coef
summary(pgls_bm)$tTable
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r,echo=F}
# OLS ignores phylogeny
ols <- lm(Y ~ X, data = dat)

# PGLS with Brownian correlation
pgls_bm <- gls(Y ~ X,
               correlation = corBrownian(phy = tree, form = ~sp),
               data = dat,
               method = "ML")

summary(ols)$coef[,3:4]
summary(pgls_bm)$tTable[,3:4]
```
]

---

# Why results can differ

OLS assumes errors are independent.  
PGLS says: "errors might be similar for close relatives."

Often:

- slope estimates can be similar
- **standard errors** can change a lot
---

# What is Brownian Motion

.pull-left[
A model of trait evoluiton that depends on:

- starting value 
- time ($t$)
- rate parameter ($\sigma^2$)

]

.pull-right[

<img src="https://lukejharmon.github.io/pcm/images/figure3-1.png" width="500">

Simulations over three different times: (A) 10, (B) 50, and (C) 100 time units.
]

---

# Part 4  

## Multivariate PGLS / Phylogenetic MANOVA

---

# Why multivariate?

Many biological traits evolve together:

- shape coordinates
- suites of linear measurements
- functionally integrated systems

If you test one variable at a time:

- you miss covariance structure
- you inflate multiple testing

---

# Two Options for MV Data

1. **Phylogenetic MANOVA**  
   - test differences among groups in multivariate space  

2. **Multivariate PGLS**  
   - multivariate response (multiple traits), predictors, and phylogeny

Different packages implement these in different ways.

---

# Example: phylogenetic MANOVA with `geomorph`

We’ll create a toy multivariate trait matrix Y (n species × p traits).

```{r}
set.seed(4)
tree2 <- rtree(80)

p <- 6 #number of characters
Y <- rbind(matrix(rnorm(40 * p),ncol=p),
           matrix(rnorm(40 * p,mean=1),ncol=p)
           )
rownames(Y) <- tree2$tip.label

group <- factor(rep(c("reef","pelagic"), each = 40))
dat2 <- data.frame(group = group)
rownames(dat2) <- tree2$tip.label

fit_mv <- procD.pgls(Y ~ group, phy = tree2, data = dat2, iter = 999)

summary(fit_mv)
```
---

# Example: phylogenetic MANOVA with `geomorph`

`summary(fit_mv)`

```{r,echo=F}
set.seed(4)
tree2 <- rtree(80)

p <- 6 #number of characters
Y <- rbind(matrix(rnorm(40 * p),ncol=p),
           matrix(rnorm(40 * p,mean=1),ncol=p)
           )
rownames(Y) <- tree2$tip.label

group <- factor(rep(c("reef","pelagic"), each = 40))
dat2 <- data.frame(group = group)
rownames(dat2) <- tree2$tip.label

fit_mv <- procD.pgls(Y ~ group, phy = tree2, data = dat2, iter = 999,print.progress = F)

summary(fit_mv)
```
---

# Interpreting multivariate tests

Pay attention to:

- the overall test (group effect)
- effect size measures (when available)
- how results look in ordination/plots (PCA)

**Significance is not the same as importance.**

---

# Visualizing MV Differences 

We can do PCA on Y just to visualize group separation.

.pull-left[
```{r,eval=F}
pcaY <- prcomp(Y, scale. = TRUE)
scY <- as_tibble(pcaY$x[,1:2]) %>%
  mutate(group = group)

ggplot(scY, aes(PC1, PC2, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.9) +
  theme_classic()
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r,echo=F}
pcaY <- prcomp(Y, scale. = TRUE)
scY <- as_tibble(pcaY$x[,1:2]) %>%
  mutate(group = group)

ggplot(scY, aes(PC1, PC2, color = group)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.9) +
  theme_classic(20)


```
*Note:* This PCA visualization does **not** “account for phylogeny”—it’s just an exploratory plot. 
]
